newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian opposition leads in presidential race.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian opposition leads in presidential race.

text.p: The main opposition candidate for Sunday's Bulgarian presidential election has an 11-point lead over the ruling Socialists but is unlikely to win on the first round, an opinion poll said on Thursday.

It said 32.5 percent of the 1,570 people polled said they would vote for lawyer Petar Stoyanov while 21.5 percent supported the Socialist candidate, Culture Minister Ivan Marazov, whose party has a majority in parliament.
Maverick politician George Ganchev, who heads the Bulgarian Business Bloc, could turn out to hold the balance of power as he was close behind Marazov on 18.5 percent.

"There are high possibilities for Ganchev reaching the second round as it is yet unclear how the 16 percent undecided voters will vote," said Tzvetan Markov, director of the Laboratory for Political Behaviour, which conducted the poll.
The poll, held a week before Bulgaria's second presidential elections since the collapse of communism forecast turnout at 74 percent. It had a three percent margin of error.

Ganchev, 57, flashy and moustachioed, represents a glamorous alternative for an electorate weighed down by falling living standards and disillusioned by bickering politicians. He won 17 percent of the vote in the 1992 presidential election.
A total of 13 are contesting the election and a second round run-off will be held on November 3 if no one wins more than 50 percent of the vote, or if turnout falls below 50 percent.
President Zhelyu Zhelev, 61, Bulgaria's first non-communist head of state, is not standing for re-election to the largely ceremonial post.

The outcome may prove crucial for Prime Minister Zhan Videnov, whose position as Bulgarian Socialist Party (BSP) leader has been shaken by his government's inability to handle the economic crisis, analysts said.

"The main battle will begin after the presidential election. For me the greatest challenge will be to get the BSP out of parliament," Ivan Kostov, leader of the opposition Union of Democratic Forces, told the daily Standard.

The former Warsaw Pact country of nine million people is in the grip of a severe economic crisis and a poverty spiral which has robbed many Bulgarians of their faith in the political system. Many say they will simply not vote.

The inflation rate is forecast to exceed 200 percent this year and the central bank is running out of money to prop up the lev and to buy fuel and wheat. Bulgarian wheat was exported because the world price was higher than the local price.
High interest rates introduced to stabilise the banking system have doubled internal debt and foreign exchange reserves have plunged to about $505 million from about $1.5 billion in the past year.

An International Monetary Fund mission is due in Sofia next week to discuss a policy framework that would allow it to release a twice-delayed $115 million second tranche of funding under Bulgaria's standby accord.
